subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: The two major systems that coordinate and integrate responses in the mammalian body are the:
questions.explain: Fast electrical (nervous) and slower chemical (endocrine) signalling together maintain coordinated control and homeostasis.

questions.q: The central nervous system consists of the:
questions.explain: The CNS integrates information; the peripheral nervous system carries signals to and from it.

questions.q: In a reflex arc, the rapid, involuntary response is possible because the signal:
options: Passes through the spinal cord without waiting for the brain
questions.explain: Reflexes route through the spinal cord for speed, protecting the body before the brain is fully aware.

questions.q: Homeostasis depends on negative feedback, in which a change in a variable triggers responses that:
options: Reverse the change and restore the set point
questions.explain: Negative feedback counteracts deviations (e.g. in temperature or blood glucose) to keep conditions stable.

questions.q: Blood glucose regulation, involving insulin and glucagon from the pancreas, is an example of:
options: Integration of endocrine control with homeostasis
questions.explain: Antagonistic hormones adjust glucose uptake and release to maintain a stable blood glucose level.

questions.q: Which is an example of a first-line, non-specific barrier to infection?
questions.explain: Physical and chemical barriers (skin, mucus, stomach acid) prevent pathogen entry as the first line of defence.

questions.q: Phagocytes defend the body by:
questions.explain: Phagocytosis is part of the innate (non-specific) immune response, ingesting and destroying microbes.

questions.q: Antibodies are produced by:
questions.explain: B lymphocytes and the plasma cells they form produce specific antibodies as part of the adaptive immune response.

questions.q: An antibody binds to a specific molecule on a pathogen called an:
questions.explain: Antibodies bind specific antigens, marking pathogens for destruction or neutralising them.

questions.q: Vaccination provides long-term protection mainly because it stimulates the formation of:
questions.explain: Memory lymphocytes allow a rapid, strong secondary response if the pathogen is encountered again.

questions.q: Antibiotics are effective against bacterial infections but not viral infections because antibiotics:
options: Target features of bacterial cells that viruses lack
questions.explain: Antibiotics disrupt bacterial structures/processes (e.g. cell walls); viruses use host cells and lack these targets.

questions.q: The overuse of antibiotics contributes to resistant bacteria because it:
options: Selects for pre-existing resistant bacteria that then reproduce
Causes bacteria to choose to mutate
Weakens the human immune system permanently
questions.explain: Antibiotics act as a selection pressure; resistant survivors pass on resistance, an example of natural selection.

questions.q: A disease that can be transmitted from other animals to humans is described as a:
questions.explain: Zoonoses (e.g. rabies, some influenzas) cross from animals to humans.

questions.q: Compared with hormonal control, nervous control of body systems is generally:
questions.explain: Nervous signals are rapid and brief; endocrine signals are slower and more sustained — the two integrate for coordination.

questions.q: Blood clotting helps defence against infection by:
options: Sealing wounds to prevent pathogen entry
questions.explain: Clot formation closes breaks in the skin, a barrier that reduces the entry of pathogens.

questions.q: A person's pupils constrict in bright light. This is best described as:
options: A nervous reflex maintaining a suitable response to the environment
questions.explain: The pupil reflex is a rapid, involuntary nervous response protecting the retina.

questions.q: HIV weakens the immune system because it destroys:
questions.explain: HIV infects and depletes helper T cells, undermining the coordination of the adaptive immune response and leading to AIDS.

questions.q: The specific, targeted immune response involving lymphocytes and antibodies is described as:
questions.explain: Adaptive immunity is specific to particular antigens and generates immunological memory.

questions.q: Effectors that carry out responses coordinated by the nervous system are typically:
questions.explain: Motor neurons stimulate effectors — muscles (movement) and glands (secretion) — to produce responses.

questions.q: Herd immunity protects unvaccinated individuals in a population because:
options: Widespread immunity reduces transmission of the pathogen
questions.explain: When enough people are immune, the pathogen cannot spread easily, indirectly protecting those who are not immune.
